Players usually alternate thumb and middle finger to pluck a repeating rhythm; in a traditional performance they may sit on a low stool and keep time with an iron ring and a string of bells on the right foot. As for forces, a male chorus occasionally accompanied the instrument in the past, and it could be joined by a curved horn (oporo or tung'), a one-string fiddle (orutu) and percussion. Modern performance often brings it together with Western instruments such as guitar, bass, keyboards and drums, a development tied to the rise of benga music.

The traditional cattle-tendon strings give a warm, deep tone, while modern nylon and fishing line make the instrument brighter and clearer. Its range spans the middle and upper register, with rich layers of overtones. The bowl-shaped wooden resonator with its cowhide soundboard gives a full resonance and a long decay, so the sound carries without losing softness. Compared with other African plucked instruments, nyatiti is closer to the elegance and depth of feeling of the classical lute; beside modern folk string instruments it combines the plain texture of an East African traditional instrument with the refinement of early European instruments, a sound that is unusual and expressive.

Nyatiti is a plucked chordophone of the Luo of western Kenya, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.21-5, a bowl-shaped yoke lute. The body is about two to three feet long, a carved wooden bowl-shaped resonator covered with cowhide; the traditional strings were cattle tendon, and nylon and fishing line are now common. Usually eight strings, tuned from top to bottom B-A-G#-E-E-D-B-A, with the outer strings in unison and the two middle strings an octave apart. The player alternately plucks with the thumb and middle finger of both hands to make a repeating rhythmic figure; traditionally the player sits on a low stool with an iron ring on the big toe of the right foot and metal bells tied to the right leg, keeping time. It is mostly a solo instrument; in the past it could be accompanied by a male chorus, or joined by curved horns, one-string fiddles and percussion, and today it is often played with guitar, bass, keyboards and drums.

The strings were made of cattle tendon in the early period; players today use almost entirely nylon and plastic fishing line. Traditional playing accessories also include a wrought-iron ring for the big toe of the right foot and metal bells on the right leg, used to keep time. Sources do not state the materials of the other parts.
尼亞蒂蒂琴起源於肯亞西部，是盧奧人的古典樂器，主要在基蘇木北部的錫亞亞地區演奏，: Nyatiti comes from western Kenya and is the classical instrument of the Luo, played mainly in the Siaya area north of Kisumu, where it carries a deep local culture. This bowl-shaped yoke lute has been handed down through Luo society from one generation to the next and is a major part of its traditional music. The body is finely made, about two to three feet long, built from a carved wooden bowl-shaped resonator and a cowhide face, and it has a sound of its own.
歷史上，琴弦採用牛腱製作，賦予樂器獨有的音色。隨著現代化進程，演奏者逐漸改用尼龍: Historically the strings were made of cattle tendon, which gave the instrument its own timbre. As modern life spread, players gradually turned to nylon and fishing line, and this change of material noticeably altered the sound of nyatiti. Nyatiti played in Kenya today usually has eight strings, more standardised than the traditional five to eight. Through folk transmission and cultural preservation the instrument has become known to a wider Kenyan society and stands as a symbol of Kenyan traditional music.
